39: This plan describes an ice cream shop that makes its own ice cream in a mid-size U.S. city of 150,000 to 300,000 people, on a neighborhood main street or next to a park or a school. The space is about 1,000 sq ft (93 sq m), with a production room of about 250 sq ft (23 sq m), dipping cabinets for {{sabores}} flavors, {{aforo}} seats inside and a patio of five tables in season, on a second-generation retail lease. It is run by an LLC: you as the ice cream maker and general manager, a shift lead all year and seasonal part-time scoopers. It opens in March, so that the summer cash carries you through the first winter, and keeps going in the cold months with ice cream cakes and holiday pies to order, hot chocolate, pints and catering. It closes for three weeks in January.
40: The key figures of the example case are these. An average of {{clientes_dia}} customers a day, each spending {{ticket}} excl. sales tax, over {{dias}} opening days, give year-1 revenue of {{ventas_a1}} and a net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}}, a net margin of {{margen_neto_a1}}. The {{clientes_dia}} customers are the average of the first year with the opening ramp-up included: the Excel spreads the year with seasonality and a start-up ramp, but the year bills what the P&L says. Break-even is at {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} customers a day, and cash break-even, which also covers the loan payments, at {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}}. This is not a guaranteed return: it is a starting point for you to change the assumptions and enter your own numbers, and a net margin this modest is honest, not a flaw.
41: Total investment is {{inversion_total}}: {{capex}} for build-out, equipment and launch (training, branding, permits and opening inventory included, plus the security deposit and the rent before opening), and {{fondo_maniobra}} of working capital. The total cash needed at opening is {{necesidad_caja}}. It is financed with {{fondos_propios}} of owner's equity ({{aportacion_pct}} of the total) and a {{prestamo}} SBA 7(a) loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, nominal and not APR, with no interest-only period. The annual loan payment is {{cuota_anual}}. Ask two lenders for a quote before you fix the rate: the plan is lender-ready, but no approval is promised.
42: Year 1 bills {{ventas_a1}} and leaves a net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}}, a net margin of {{margen_neto_a1}}. Customers grow {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3 at the same average check, so revenue moves to {{ventas_a2}} and {{ventas_a3}} and net profit to {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}. The cash margin over cash break-even is {{holgura_caja_pct}}, and the DSCR never drops below {{dscr_min}}, against a lender limit of {{dscr_limite}} used by the workbook. The project pays back before debt in {{payback}}. That net margin is far below the 10-25% figures that circulate online, and the plan shows why: hourly wages, a short season and a purchased base weigh on the result.
43: The team is small and leans on you. You are the ice cream maker and you batch-freeze the ice cream every day in the production room. A shift lead works all year, and seasonal part-time scoopers join with the season, in a team of {{plantilla_puestos}} positions (relief cover included) that add up to {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents. The kit includes this ten-section business plan, the nine-tab Excel financial projections, the 80-task startup checklist in six phases and the equivalents guide for the U.S., UK, Canada and Australia.
46: Not every ice cream shop is the same business, and it pays to choose before you sign anything. A scoop shop that makes its own ice cream controls the product and puts the work in view, but it needs the biggest investment and more health-department steps. A shop that only resells finished ice cream starts with less money, but leaves the margin and the difference in the supplier's hands. A soft serve or frozen yogurt counter sells a different product with different equipment. A seasonal kiosk costs little and lives on one good spot and a few months. A franchise brings a brand and a method in exchange for fees and little freedom over the menu. Each model has its own investment, permits and margin, and this plan takes the first one because it builds a product of your own.
47: The value proposition is ice cream made here in small batches, every day, that the customer can watch from the counter. There are {{sabores}} flavors in summer and 10-12 in winter: the classics, the seasonal ones, a signature flavor or two and dairy-free sorbets for guests who avoid milk. The case buys a pasteurized ice cream base from a licensed dairy and finishes it in the shop: you flavor it, add the mix-ins, batch-freeze it, harden it and serve it from the dipping cabinets. After the dairy's pasteurization you add only flavorings and mix-ins: no raw eggs, no raw milk or cream, and custard flavors need a custard base. Making your own mix is a variant that requires a state license and other equipment; ask your state department of agriculture. Names are honest: you call it ice cream or frozen custard only if the recipe meets 21 CFR 135.110, and you write "made here in small batches", not "homemade", unless it is true. Allergens are handled at the cabinet and on the menu, and you never promise allergen-free.
48: The example menu is simple, in prices excl. sales tax (Kit estimate, Oct 2026): a single scoop at $5.25, a double at $7.00, a kid's scoop at $4.25, a waffle cone for $1.25 more, a sundae at $9.00, a pint at $11, a quart at $18, an 8-inch ice cream cake at $45, an espresso at $3.50 and a hot chocolate at $4.50. Sales split as follows: ice cream in all its forms (scoops, sundaes, pints, cakes and catering) is {{comida_pct}} of the total, and coffee and drinks are {{bebida_pct}}. Use the prices of your own area: there is no reliable national average for the price of a scoop.
49: The average check in the case is {{ticket}} per person excl. sales tax, or {{precio_menu}} incl. sales tax. It is per person, not per register ticket: one ticket often covers more than one person. With that check, the cost of goods sold weighs {{cogs_pct}} of sales and the gross margin is {{margen_bruto_pct}}. It pays to watch the customer and not the ticket, because the Excel grows customers at the same average check instead of raising prices. One gesture that does move the check is offering a pint, a sundae or a topping at the register.
50: Winter is part of the concept, not a pause. There is no equipment that needs a smoke exhaust: the shop runs on ice cream cakes to order, holiday pies and pints, hot chocolate and catering, and it closes three weeks in January and on Mondays from November to February. With that menu the shop stays alive, the year-round team has work and the summer cash is not spent entirely before spring.
53: Demand for ice cream in the United States is large and strongly seasonal. According to the International Dairy Foods Association (IDFA), July is the month with the most ice cream production, and the country dedicates a whole month to it: in 1984, Presidential Proclamation 5219 declared July National Ice Cream Month and the third Sunday of July National Ice Cream Day. Your market is not the pint people buy at the supermarket, but the ice cream they prefer to buy fresh, at the counter, from someone who makes it. This plan does not use household consumption figures it could not verify: replace them with what you see on your own street.
54: Seasonality is marked. Industry estimates, such as those from 7shifts, put summer sales up to 40% above the average and winter about 30% below it. The peak season runs from Memorial Day to Labor Day. Scoop prices vary by region, so compare your menu with the shops within a mile or two of yours rather than with a national average, and test the example prices against your neighborhood.
55: Searches show a market where the final customer leads. According to DataForSEO, in October 2026 the term "ice cream shop business plan" has 320 searches a month in the U.S., "opening an ice cream shop" 320, "homemade ice cream shop" 2,400, with a peak in summer, and "ice cream shop equipment" 1,000. People who want to open a shop look for a plan, for the cost and for the license, so the little they find has to be useful with its own numbers. That is why this plan comes with an Excel you can recalculate with your city and your rent instead of generic promises.
56: With Month 1 in March, the plan spreads sales with seasonality: most of the revenue lands between April and September, with the peak in July (Month 5) and the valley in January. The start-up carries a ramp-up that begins below full pace and reaches cruising speed after a few months. The lowest cash balance of year 1, {{saldo_minimo}}, comes in Month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}, just after the investment is paid; then the summer lifts it. That is why you open in March: opening in the fall would spend the working capital before the first July. The "12-Month Cash Flow" tab shows it month by month.
57: The gap is clear: the first Google results for an ice cream shop business plan are mostly blog guides and generic templates, rarely a Word plan with a live Excel that models summer seasonality and a startup checklist to go with it. This document is built to fill that gap, with an example case that you recalculate for your city.
58: Demand has risks that the plan names. The season is short: a rainy spring or a cool summer shows up in the register. A price war on the scoop and supermarket ice cream at home press on the average check. And local rules on patio seating and sidewalk space limit what you can sell outside the season, so check them with your city.
61: Before you set any price, draw the map of who competes with you in your neighborhood and your city. In ice cream, competition comes from seven sides: supermarket ice cream, franchises, other scoop shops, gelato-style shops, coffee shops and dessert counters that sell bought-in ice cream, seasonal kiosks and delivery apps. Each one takes customers for a different reason, which is why it pays to look at them one by one, as follows.
62: Porter's five forces look like this for an ice cream shop with a production room. The bargaining power of suppliers is moderate: milk, cream, sugar and fruit are bought from several places, but pastes, swirls and the equipment depend on a few brands, and the base depends on the licensed dairies near you. The power of customers is high, because they change shops in an afternoon and compare the scoop from one street to the next. The threat of new entrants is medium: opening a shop is easy if you resell finished ice cream, but with your own production room the investment, the permits and the craft slow people down. The threat of substitutes is high: supermarket ice cream, dessert shops, coffee, shakes, fruit or any dessert. Rivalry is strong in summer and almost absent in winter, when many shops close. So the advantage is in the product, the service and in knowing what you do when the temperature drops.
63: Direct competitors are other scoop shops, from the neighborhood and downtown, and the gelato-style shops, where gelato is a style, with less fat and overrun and served a little warmer. Behind them come the franchises, with a brand and a storefront. On the substitute side are supermarket ice cream, coffee shops and dessert counters that serve bought-in ice cream, seasonal kiosks and delivery apps with ice cream brands. Your answer is not to lower the price: it is to show the production room, serve the flavor of the day and justify the difference.
64: The barriers to entry are compliance and cash. The first is the license decision: buying a pasteurized base from a licensed dairy usually makes you a retail food establishment, while making your own mix means a state dairy plant or frozen dessert manufacturer license and 3-A equipment. It depends on your state: ask your state department of agriculture and your local health department before you buy equipment. The health permit comes after plan review and an inspection, and the patio needs its own sidewalk café permit. And cash weighs: the machines, the furniture and the equipment of the case add up to a large part of the {{capex}} of startup costs. Confirm each step with your city, your county and your CPA.
65: Four factors decide whether it works. The first is the product: ice cream that is different every day, with honest names and seasonal flavors. The second is the site: a street with foot traffic and a shop that can be seen. The third is cost control: cost of goods sold in the case is {{cogs_pct}} of year-1 sales and cash break-even is at {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}} customers a day, so every scoop that is given away or thrown out shows. The fourth is the winter cash: keep it from the first summer and do not spend it on the first whim.
66: The SWOT of this concept is clear. Strengths: a production room in view, the flavor of the day, honest names and a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}} in year 1. Weaknesses: a high investment and a cash flow very sensitive to the season. Opportunities: ice cream cakes and holiday pies to order, catering, and pints to go. Threats: a price war on the scoop, supermarket ice cream at home, cool summers and local rules on the patio and sidewalk space. The defense is in the product, the experience, the pint to go and the pre-orders, which are paid in advance.
69: The marketing strategy follows the seasons, because the business does too. March opens with a tasting for the neighborhood, the schools and the nearby shops, and an Opening Day. From April to September, and especially from Memorial Day to Labor Day, the flavor of the day, the patio and the cake orders lead; National Ice Cream Day, the third Sunday of July, is a natural promotion. In September you prepare the winter, with the cakes, holiday pies and pints, and hot chocolate. Every month has one concrete action, and none depends on the budget of a big brand.
70: Social media is the shop window of the flavor of the day. Post the flavor of the day every morning, the production room while you batch-freeze, the finished cakes and the seasonal novelties. Photos and short videos shot in the shop work better than catalog pictures, and consistency matters more than perfection. A simple website with the menu, the allergens, the hours and an order form for cakes completes the window, because the customer looks at it before coming. Link both to your Google Business Profile, so that anyone who searches for an ice cream shop in your city finds you and sees you make it.
71: The Google Business Profile is your best free ad, because almost everyone who looks for an ice cream shop nearby checks it. Complete it with photos of the shop, the production room and the cabinets, and update the hours for each season: summer, winter and the three-week closing in January. Answer every review, the bad ones too, kindly and without arguing. Ask the happy customer to leave an opinion when they pick up a pint, not later. Over time, the profile is what decides who walks in.
72: Local outreach starts at your door. Hold a tasting for the neighborhood and bring samples with tasting spoons to schools, daycares, shops and offices nearby. For restaurants and cafés in town, your own ice cream is a dessert they do not have: offer a trial, a clear price and a regular service, but first ask your state department of agriculture what license, labeling and inspections apply to selling to other businesses. It is a small channel, a modest part of the case's sales, but a steady and predictable one that helps carry the winter.
73: Orders are the sale you know in advance. Ice cream cakes for birthdays all year, for graduations in May and June, for the Fourth of July and holiday pies and cakes in November and December are booked ahead with a deposit. On summer evenings, pints and quarts can be sold through DoorDash or Uber Eats; in the case, delivery is {{delivery_pct}} of sales, with a commission of {{comision_pct}}, so set a minimum order and a price that absorbs the commission. Delivery adds to the sale; it does not replace the shop.
74: Loyalty can be simple. A paper punch card or a flavor club by text message to announce the new flavor is enough to bring customers back. No conversion rates are estimated here, because they depend on your neighborhood and on how you work at it: measure them yourself during the first summer. The best marketing is the flavor of the day, a friendly welcome and a customer who remembers your name and you theirs.
75: The marketing budget in the case is {{marketing_anual}} a year, mostly for photography, local ads and the tasting materials. Branding, the website, the photos and the launch go separately, inside the startup costs. The first winter is worked from September, with the winter menu already announced and the holiday orders open. Honest claims count: write "made here in small batches" on the sign, and "homemade" only if it is true.
